rule_provenance.rule: When constructing a two-strain E. coli consortium with a defined ecological interaction, reconfigure cis- vs trans-acting QS activation of a shared toxin-antitoxin effect module, because assigning self-HSL to antitoxin and partner-HSL to toxin yields competition whereas the inverse assignment yields symbiosis (validated in E. coli Top10 QS-ccd proof-of-concept consortia).

When engineering a two-strain E. coli mutualism from a QS-ccd toolkit, assign each strain's own HSL to toxin expression and the partner's HSL to antitoxin expression, because this converts aggression into suicidal behavior that is rescued only by the partner, yielding obligate-like mutual protection (validated for the SG01/SR01 E. coli Top10 pair in LB liquid and agar).

When externally tunable subpopulation ratios are needed in a QS-based two-strain E. coli consortium, replace the self-inducing QS promoters of the HSL synthases with orthogonal inducible promoters (Ara/aTc), because inducer dosage then sets signal production, which propagates through the toxin-antitoxin feedbacks to set the steady-state strain ratio (validated in E. coli Top10 competitive and symbiotic ecosystems at 1.5 mL scale).

When monitoring two E. coli subpopulations in coculture, integrate distinguishable fluorescent reporters into the chromosome (e.g., CRIM method) and use fluorescence rather than OD600 as the growth readout, because OD600 cannot resolve strains and is biased by dead cells (validated in LB liquid and agar cocultures of QS-ccd ecosystems).
